Scientometrics · citation simulation · report 1

Can search behaviour explain the citation distribution?

Experiments run on 20 November 2026 · corpus: AMiner DBLP v10 (850,406 papers) · code: github.com/megaduks/scientometrics
Summary1 · Hypothesis2 · Input data 3 · The inherited code4 · Simulation model5 · Experimental plan 6.1 · Pilot runs6.2 · Stage 16.3 · Stage 2 6.4 · Candidate pool6.5 · Formal tests7 · Interpretation 8 · Limitations9 · Further researchAppendices

Summary

  • body reproducedA simulated researcher who searches by topic, ranks results partly by citation count, and cites from the first one or two result pages reproduces the empirical citation distribution up to about the 99.9th percentile. The best settings leave about 35% of papers never cited (empirical: 36.3%), and the largest gap between the cumulative distributions is 0.014.
  • tail not reproducedAll four formal tests from the collaborators' plan reject every shortlisted setting (8 settings × 3 seeds). Above xmin = 88 the simulated tails are steeper (α̂ = 2.90–4.80 against α₀ = 2.78) and curved like a log-normal, while the empirical tail is a straight power law. The most-cited simulated paper reaches 3,034 citations at most; the real one has 4,420.
  • The key ingredients are realistic topics (queries taken from real titles, not from a fixed word list) and a moderate citation weight (0.30–0.35 when counts accumulate during the simulation, 0.40 with real counts). The citing rule, page size, recency and venue weights matter much less.
  • Enlarging the search result pool from 500 to 2,000 candidates roughly doubles the most-cited count and moves the tail exponent towards the empirical value. This suggests the remaining gap comes from limited exposure: a paper can only be cited by queries that retrieve it.
  • The original student code could not be used: the generator that produced the earlier simulated data is lost, and the surviving version ranked the least similar papers first. Everything here comes from a rewritten, tested generator (citesim).

1Hypothesis and research question

The hypothesis is that the heavy-tailed distribution of citations is, to a large extent, a product of how researchers find what they cite. A researcher writing a paper searches a scholarly search engine (such as Google Scholar) with keywords related to the paper. They then cite a few papers from the first result page, fewer from the second page, and so on. The engine's ranking mixes topical relevance with signals such as recency, citation count and venue prestige.

Real Google Scholar cannot be queried at scale, so the process is simulated on a real database of computer-science papers. Many hypothetical new papers each run a search, re-rank the results by a weighted score, paginate them, and cite papers from the top pages. The citations they generate form a simulated citation distribution.

Research question. Is the simulated distribution of citations the same as the empirical one? Only the shape of the distribution matters, not which particular papers get cited.

The statistical comparison follows the plan in the e-mail from the Institute of Mathematics (PUT). Treat the empirical tail as a fully specified Pareto/power law. Test the simulated tails against it with Anderson-Darling (sensitive in the tails). Then test the exponent with a likelihood-ratio test, and compare the power law with a log-normal using Vuong's test.

2Input data

Corpus. The AMiner citation network, DBLP version 10, holds 3,079,007 computer-science papers with titles, years, venues and reference lists. Papers are kept only if their venue exactly matches an entry on the Polish ministry list of journals and conferences, which also provides a venue score (20–200 points). This leaves 850,406 papers published between 1936 and 2018. The subset is intentional: it is the database the simulated researchers search.

Choosing the empirical target. AMiner provides a citation count per paper (n_citation), but it has two problems. First, it counts citations from the whole literature, not from the corpus being searched. Second, it uses 50 as a placeholder for unknown counts: 251,797 papers (29.6%) have exactly 50 (Figure 1A). Papers with the placeholder are cited only 2.3 times on average from inside the corpus. The target is therefore the number of times each paper is cited by other papers in the corpus, counted from their reference lists. It lives in the same closed world as the simulation and has no artefacts. On a log scale it correlates 0.87 with n_citation (placeholder excluded).

3Starting point: the inherited code

The project started from a master's thesis repository (J. Fiturski) with four notebooks and two files of results: source_distribution.csv (empirical) and distribution_citations.csv (306 simulated distributions). The audit found that the results cannot be trusted or reproduced.

The repository was cleaned of unused template code and moved to megaduks/scientometrics. The generator was then rewritten from scratch as a tested Python package (Section 4). Appendix A records what the legacy files show, for completeness.

4The simulation model (citesim)

  1. Hypothetical papers. A run writes N new papers (default N = 850,406, one per corpus paper). Each borrows a real "source" paper, which supplies its title for title queries and its reference count where needed.
  2. Query. Either a generated keyword query, of the form “{verb-ing} {adjective} {noun} {agent}” (e.g. “Optimizing Distributed Query Scheduler”), built from four word lists of 100, 100, 182 and 100 words; or the source paper's real title, with the source paper excluded from its own results.
  3. Search. Titles and queries are embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (unit vectors). Exact cosine search over the whole corpus on the GPU keeps the top M candidates (M = 500 or 2,000).
  4. Ranking. The candidates are re-ranked by a weighted score. Each feature is min-max scaled within the candidate set, so the weights are comparable:
score = w_sim·similarity + w_rec·recency(year) + w_cit·log(1 + citations) + w_ven·venue points
  1. Citation signal. Static ranks by the papers' real within-corpus counts, as a search engine shows them today. Dynamic ranks by citations received so far from the run's own hypothetical papers, starting from zero (a rich-get-richer feedback). Hypothetical papers are processed in random order.
  2. Pagination and citing. The ranked list is cut into pages of 10 or 20. Each paper cites distinct papers chosen at random within each page, following a citing rule: [5] means five from page 1; [3,1,1] means three, one and one from pages 1–3; [2,1,1,1] and [1,1,1,1,1] spread citations further. Every rule cites 5 papers, close to the real mean of 4.93 in-corpus references.
  3. Output. Citation counts for all 850,406 papers, including zeros. The results are compared with the empirical target.

Each run is seeded and stores its parameters. The package has 17 unit tests covering, for example, that similarity ranks the most similar paper first, that no paper is cited twice by the same hypothetical paper, that runs are reproducible, and that the goodness-of-fit test holds its level. An optional --dated mode restricts each search to papers no newer than the source paper; it was used only in the pilot runs.

5Experimental plan

The experiment ran in stages, each one narrowing the parameter space for the next. The shape distance used for screening is the largest absolute gap between the simulated and empirical CCDFs, evaluated on a log-spaced grid from 1 to 10,000 citations (0 = identical).

6Results

6.1 Pilot: generated queries versus title queries

Both pilot runs used the same settings: weights (0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1), page 10, [3,1,1], dynamic citation counts, with search restricted to earlier papers. They produce almost the same number of citations but opposite shapes (Figure 2). With generated queries the citations pile onto few papers: 79% are never cited, and the five most-cited papers are all about debugging, because the 482-word vocabulary is dominated by software-engineering terms. With real titles as queries the citations spread far too evenly: the most-cited paper gets 270 citations.

Title queries4,252,00226.0%4690270

How well does topical search recover real citations? For 20,000 sampled papers the paper's own title was used as the query and the 500 results were compared with its real reference list. Only 38.6% of the real in-corpus references appear in the top 500. Of those, 22.3% are on page 1 (top 10) and 37.3% in the top 30; the median rank is 61. With the time-restricted search the share was 44%. Topical similarity of titles explains part of real citing, but most references are not among the most similar titles.

6.2 Stage 1: query source and citation weight

From here on, every hypothetical paper searches the whole database. The citation weight is the main dial (Figure 4). Without it, title queries spread citations too thin (about 10% never cited). At high weight, citations concentrate on a few papers (over 80% never cited). The empirical shape falls between, at about w_cit = 0.25 with dynamic counts or 0.5 with static counts. No weight rescues the generated queries: their best run still leaves 77% of papers uncited, and adding citation weight only makes it worse. The four settings without a citation term produced identical static and dynamic runs, which serves as a reproducibility check.

6.3 Stage 2: refining weights, citing rule and page size

Stage 2 used title queries only. It narrows the citation weight to a clear optimum: 0.30–0.35 with dynamic counts and 0.40 with static counts (Figure 5). Within that optimum, flatter citing rules ([5] and [1,1,1,1,1]) beat [3,1,1], and 20 results per page is slightly better than 10 (Figure 6). Across the stage-2 design, the median distance by citing rule is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1] 0.092, [2, 1, 1, 1] 0.103, [3, 1, 1] 0.110, [5] 0.094; by signal it is dynamic 0.084 and static 0.147. Recency and venue weights change the median distance by less than 0.01. The best settings reach a shape distance of 0.014. One setting gets the 99.9th percentile almost exactly (262 vs 263) but still stops at 997 citations for its most-cited paper.

6.4 Candidate pool: 500 versus 2,000 results

All stage-1 and stage-2 runs have one thing in common: their most-cited paper falls far short of the empirical 4,420. One explanation is exposure. A paper can only be cited by queries that put it among their M candidates. Repeating the 28 weight vectors with M = 2,000 tests this (Figure 7). The most-cited count rises by a median factor of 2.15, and the highest value across runs grows from 1,123 to 3,034. For dynamic settings near the optimum, the shape distance also improves (best 0.018–0.020 at [3,1,1] against 0.021–0.047 at M = 500). Static settings get worse, because the larger pool also concentrates citations.

6.5 Formal tests on the shortlist

Shortlist. The 8 settings with the smallest shape distance (6 with M = 500, 2 with M = 2,000), each run with 3 seeds, give 24 runs in total.

Null model. The tail of the empirical target is fitted once with a discrete power law, P(x) = x−α / ζ(α, xmin) for x ≥ xmin, with xmin chosen by the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman KS method. The fitted values are then treated as true: xmin = 88, α₀ = 2.785 ± 0.029, with 3,814 papers in the tail. The empirical tail fits its own law very well (A² = 0.19, p = 0.99; optimistic, because the parameters come from the same data). Vuong's test cannot separate it from a log-normal (R = -0.83, p = 0.41).

Tests per run (Benjamini-Hochberg across the 24 runs, separately per test):

  1. Anderson-Darling against the fully specified law. Citation counts are integers with many ties, so a continuous A-D gives infinite statistics. The discrete A² of Choulakian, Lockhart and Stephens (1994) is used instead, with a 999-sample Monte Carlo null. Under H0 it rejected 8.0% at the 5% level (100 replicates), so it is slightly liberal.
  2. Likelihood-ratio test of α = α₀ against a freely estimated α, compared with χ²(1).
  3. Vuong's test of power law against log-normal on the tail above xmin (non-nested).
  4. Two-sample Anderson-Darling between the simulated and empirical tails, with no model assumed (999 permutations).

Result: every run is rejected by every test. The A² values range from 11 to 520, far above anything the null produces. Figure 8 shows why: the simulated curves follow the empirical one closely up to roughly 100–200 citations, then bend down and stop between about 380 and 1,300 citations, while the empirical tail continues straight to 4,420. Every simulated exponent is above α₀, and Vuong favours the log-normal in all 24 runs (Figure 9). The two settings with the 2,000 pool come closest (α̂ = 2.92 and 2.99; A² 12–16). The static settings, which match the body best, have the worst tails.

7Interpretation

What the search mechanism explains. Three ingredients are enough to reproduce the bulk of the empirical distribution, about 99.5% of all papers. Researchers search by the topic of their own paper. The engine boosts already-cited papers moderately (the citation term carries about a third of the weight). Researchers cite fairly evenly from the first one or two pages. The never-cited share, the median and the 99th percentile all match. The citation feedback is essential: without it, citations spread too evenly; with too much of it, a few papers absorb everything. The topical structure is also essential: a narrow, artificial query vocabulary cannot be compensated by any ranking.

What it does not explain. The extreme tail, the few hundred papers with more than ~300 citations, does not emerge. The simulated tails bend in a log-normal way. This is the pattern expected when growth is multiplicative but each item's exposure is capped. Here a paper's audience is limited to the queries for which it is topically among the top M results, and the citation boost reorders papers only within that pool. Enlarging the pool moved the tail in the right direction, which supports this reading. The empirical classics (SIFT, LIBSVM, Random Forests, the SVM paper) are general-purpose methods cited from almost every subfield; their titles are not similar to the titles of the papers that cite them.

Answer to the research question. On the evidence so far, the simulated and empirical distributions are not the same. The formal tests reject equality for every setting tried. Search-and-paginate behaviour with citation-boosted ranking is a sufficient explanation for the body of the distribution, but not for its power-law tail. An additional mechanism that gives some papers audience beyond their topic seems necessary.

8Limitations and threats to validity

  • Closed world. Both the target and the simulation count only citations within the 850k-paper subset defined by the ministry venue list. Results may differ for the full literature.
  • Titles as topics. Queries and documents are represented by titles only, embedded with a small sentence model. Abstracts would give a richer topical signal; only 38.6% of real references appear in a title search's top 500.
  • Static ranking reads the target. Static runs rank by the real within-corpus counts, so the target enters the simulation. Dynamic runs avoid this, and they match better.
  • Fixed citing volume. Every hypothetical paper cites exactly 5 papers. Real reference lists vary (mean 4.93, 22% cite nothing in the corpus).
  • Exposure cap. Only the top M = 500 or 2,000 results per query are ever ranked. This is a computational shortcut that, as shown above, shapes the tail.
  • Test sensitivity. With 3,000–5,300 papers in each tail, the tests detect small differences. The effect sizes (Δα, the CCDF gap) should be read together with the p-values. The Monte Carlo A-D test is slightly liberal (8% at the 5% level), which does not affect any decision.
  • One random query set. Generated queries used one seed; title queries are deterministic. Query-sampling variability was not measured.

9Further research

  1. Test the exposure explanation directly. Run the best dynamic settings with M = 5,000 and with an uncapped citation channel. One version: rank globally by citations a fraction of the time. Another: re-rank the full result list rather than the top M. If the tail straightens, the hypothesis needs only a broader ranking, not a new mechanism. An M = 5,000 cache needs about 25 GB; 37 GB is free.
  2. Add a “classics” channel. Let a small share of citations go to papers found through a topic-independent route (most-cited lists, surveys, textbooks, citing what others cite). Estimate the share that straightens the tail, and test whether it is plausible.
  3. Model citation copying. Cite some papers from the reference lists of papers already chosen (the Simkin-Roychowdhury mechanism). Copying is a known source of power-law tails and is close to how researchers actually work.
  4. Richer topical representation. Use abstracts for embeddings and multi-query searches per paper. Measure how much of the real reference list each variant recovers, and calibrate against it.
  5. Realistic citing volume. Draw each hypothetical paper's number of citations from the empirical reference-count distribution, and let the citing rule scale with it.
  6. Time dynamics. Run the dated mode with dynamic counts in true chronological order, and compare the simulated and real citation trajectories of individual cohorts, not only the final distribution.
  7. Formal inference over parameters. Replace grid screening with approximate Bayesian computation or a surrogate model. Use the CCDF gap and the tail statistics as summaries, to obtain a posterior over weights and rules and a principled model comparison.
  8. Generated queries. If the original keyword design is to stay in the study, build the word lists from the corpus titles themselves (thousands of words, weighted by frequency), so that queries cover the database the way real topics do.

AAppendix A: analyses of the legacy data

Before the generator was rewritten, the tests from the e-mail were also run on the inherited files: the empirical distribution was AMiner n_citation with the placeholder dropped, and the simulated data were the 306 legacy distributions. They were run as test cases for a reusable testing procedure. The results are recorded here, but the legacy simulations come from unknown, buggy code, so they carry no evidential weight.

Test (legacy data)Result
Empirical tail (n_citation, 50s dropped)x_min = 587, α = 2.58 ± 0.02, 5,314 papers; power law vs log-normal not separable (Vuong p ≈ 0.24–0.27)
Anderson-Darling vs fully specified Pareto306 / 306 runs rejected
LR test of α = α₀283–290 / 306 runs rejected; 16–23 runs (mostly rows 10–32) consistent
Vuong, power law vs log-normal (6 sampled runs)log-normal favoured in 5–6 / 6

These runs also showed two technical points for any analysis of citation counts. First, continuous tests fail on integer data with ties at xmin, so discrete versions are needed. Second, the powerlaw package caps α at 3 by default, so steep tails must be fitted with a wider range. Both are handled in citesim.gof.
